note: Turns the Act pillars into 22 metrics and shows accuracy and compliance can diverge, which is a useful result for scoring an engagement.
title: Towards Quantifying Compliance with the EU AI Act
journal: Proceedings of the Annual Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences
explain_beginner: The EU AI Act sets ethical rules for AI in five areas: explainability, fairness, privacy, robustness, and social and environmental well-being. This paper turns those five areas into 22 measurable scores, so compliance can be checked in a repeatable way. The authors tested their scoring method on three standard classification tasks. They found that an AI can be very accurate yet still fail compliance expectations. Bigger datasets helped robustness but made privacy leakage worse. Some fairness and explainability scores overlapped, so they could be simplified, while social and environmental measures were the least developed.
explain_business: This work offers a way to score AI systems against the EU AI Act using 22 concrete metrics across five ethical areas. For leaders, the key finding is that strong accuracy does not mean compliance, so accuracy alone is a poor proxy for regulatory readiness. Dataset size also involves a trade-off: it can improve robustness but raise privacy risk. The framework could inform build, buy, or audit decisions, and it suggests fairness and explainability reporting may be streamlined, while privacy and social and environmental measures need more investment before they can be trusted.
explain_practitioner: The authors propose a structured, score-based framework that operationalizes the EU AI Act's five pillars into 22 interpretable metrics, enabling reproducible, model-agnostic compliance assessment. They applied it to three benchmark tabular classification tasks using a standardized deep learning model. Results show dataset characteristics shape ethical performance: high predictive accuracy does not guarantee compliance, and larger datasets improve robustness while increasing privacy leakage vulnerability. Correlation analyses reveal redundancy among fairness and explainability metrics, suggesting simplification is possible, whereas privacy metrics remain essential and diverse. Social and environmental measures are least mature, indicating a need for novel, bounded metrics.
